strengths: Introduces a novel and timely task—detecting paper-code discrepancies—and releases SciCOQA, a dataset of 611 discrepancies (81 real, 530 synthetic) with a clear taxonomy of discrepancy types and categories, addressing reproducibility and scientific quality assurance.

The data collection pipeline is carefully designed: real-world discrepancies come from GitHub issues and reproducibility papers with manual filtering, while synthetic discrepancies are generated from real repositories and analyzed for code-change minimality, file diversity, and programming-language distribution.

The benchmark is extensive, covering 21 LLMs across commercial and open-weight families, with analyses by discrepancy origin, type, context length, publication year, programming language, and a code-only ablation, providing a useful picture of current model limitations.

The paper is transparent about its limitations and ethical considerations, and reproducibility is supported through dataset/code links, prompts, model versions, context-processing details, and versioned paper/code snapshots.

Results are clearly presented: GPT-5 achieves the best real-world recall at 45.7%, while models struggle most with paper omissions and longer inputs; the synthetic/real recall correlation (r = 0.94) and unlabeled-prediction precision analysis add useful supporting evidence.
weaknesses: The ground truth for real discrepancies is partly GPT-5-generated and GPT-5-validated rather than fully human-written, raising potential circularity and model-bias concerns for both dataset labels and evaluation.

The synthetic subset (530 of 611 discrepancies) is generated by GPT-5 without human validation of label correctness; this risks noisy or unrealistic labels and may bias results toward GPT-5, which also performs best on the synthetic data.
The real-world subset is small (81 discrepancies from 67 papers) and skewed toward CS/AI, so conclusions about non-CS domains rely heavily on synthetic data and should be treated cautiously.

Evaluation uses an LLM-as-a-judge (GPT-OSS 20B) that is also one of the benchmarked models; although the judge was validated on 20 discrepancies, the setup may still introduce self-preference or stylistic bias.

There is no human upper-bound performance or inter-annotator agreement for the manual filtering, discrepancy typing, or category labeling, leaving the reliability of the ground truth incompletely quantified.
Precision analysis is limited to 12 NLP papers and pooled ground truth; a fuller false-positive analysis across the real dataset would strengthen the evaluation.

Some broader claims—e.g., synthetic data as a reliable proxy and publication-year effects as evidence of contamination—are supported mainly by correlational analysis rather than controlled experiments.

strengths: Introduces a novel and timely task: detecting paper-code discrepancies in scientific publications, extending code-comment inconsistency and scientific error detection to cross-modal, repository-scale alignment.

Presents SciCoQA, a carefully constructed dataset of 611 discrepancies combining real-world examples from GitHub issues and reproducibility papers with synthetic scaling, including detailed taxonomy, examples, versioned code links, and public release.

Provides a comprehensive empirical study of 21 LLMs with analyses by origin, discrepancy type/category, context length, publication year, code-only ablation, and precision validation, yielding actionable insights such as best real-world recall only 45.7%, paper omissions being hardest, and the paper being necessary for the task.
High reproducibility: releases data/code, provides full prompts, model versions, context windows, versioning strategy, and implementation details; includes limitations and ethical considerations.
weaknesses: The real-world evaluation set is small (81 discrepancies from 67 papers), so headline performance claims (e.g., GPT-5 recall 45.7%) lack confidence intervals or significance tests and may be statistically fragile.

Synthetic discrepancies are generated by GPT-5 and represent 87% of the dataset; although the paper shows high rank correlation with real data, synthetic items are easier (71.3% vs 45.7% recall) and may not match the distribution or difficulty of real-world discrepancies.

Ground-truth construction and prediction matching rely heavily on LLM-based extraction/verification and an LLM-as-a-judge; despite manual filtering and precision validation on 12 NLP papers, the subjective boundary of a 'meaningful discrepancy' may introduce label noise, and no inter-annotator agreement is reported.

Domain diversity is partly synthetic: real-world data is predominantly CS/AI, while non-CS domains are synthetic, so claims about broad computational science applicability are not fully validated with real examples.

Evaluation focuses on recall; precision is validated only on a small subset, and the recall metric likely underestimates models by treating valid unannotated predictions as misses, making the headline 'only 45.7%' difficult to interpret without a human upper bound or baseline.

strengths: Introduces a novel and timely task: detecting paper-code discrepancies for scientific quality assurance and reproducibility.
Constructs SciCOQA, a dataset with 81 real and 530 synthetic discrepancies, including a taxonomy of discrepancy types and categories.
Benchmarks 21 LLMs, revealing that even the best model (GPT-5) detects only 45.7% of real-world discrepancies, underscoring the task's difficulty.
Provides extensive analyses (code-only ablation, context length effects, publication year, programming language) and releases data/code under open licenses.
Transparently discusses limitations and ethical considerations, including data licensing and automation risks.
weaknesses: Real-world data is small (81 discrepancies) and skewed toward CS/AI; the abstract overclaims diversity by including synthetic non-CS data without clearly qualifying that these are not real-world instances.

Synthetic discrepancies are generated by GPT-5 and used as ground truth without human verification; the reported correlation (r=0.94) with real performance is weak evidence of realism and may be confounded by model capabilities.

The evaluation metric for recall only examines the top-3 most similar predictions per model (via embedding similarity), likely underestimating true recall and biasing results; no sensitivity analysis for this design choice is provided.

Annotation reliability is not established: no inter-annotator agreement or details on the number/qualifications of human annotators for filtering and validation, leaving the ground truth potentially subjective.

The definition of 'paper-code discrepancy' is narrow, excluding bugs, hyperparameter mismatches, and documentation nits, which limits the benchmark's scope and its ability to capture the full spectrum of reproducibility issues.

Potential circularity: GPT-5 is used for synthetic data generation and is also the best-performing evaluated model, while GPT-OSS 20B serves as the judge; these overlapping roles may introduce uncontrolled biases.
